title: ‘Coven Academy’ Creator Breaks Down Briar’s Family Tree, Dark Magic as an Addiction Metaphor, ‘Misogyny’ Against Witches — and a Deleted Kiss Scene
description:

	‘Coven Academy’ Creator Breaks Down Briar’s Family Tree, Dark Magic as an Addiction Metaphor, ‘Misogyny’ Against
body:
Oct 3, 2026 11:00am PT	
	

	
	‘Coven Academy’ Creator Breaks Down Briar’s Family Tree, Dark Magic as an Addiction Metaphor, ‘Misogyny’ Against Witches — and a Deleted Kiss Scene
	



			
			
	
						

									Disney/David Astorga
	
					


							
		
	SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “Coven Academy,” now streaming on Disney+.

	“Coven Academy” was supposed to be the first true young adult drama in the history of Disney Channel. The series, set at a New Orleans boarding school for witches and warlocks, is bloodier and darker than the network ever got with other magical fare like “Wizards of Waverly Place.”

	Ultimately, those qualities drove Disney to decide “Coven Academy” would be more at home on Freeform. “I think this shares more DNA with a classic CW show like ‘Vampire Diaries,’ or even the ‘Sabrina’ revival on on Netflix,” says series creator Tim Federle, best known as the mind behind “High School Musical: The Musical: The Series.” “When we went to Vancouver to shoot this, I feel like I hired half the ‘Riverdale’ team and was like, ‘Let’s bring that aesthetic to this show.’ Optically and message-wise, this sits in a different space than Disney Channel. As more and more of the higher ups at the company watched the show and got excited, there was a decision made, which was that this doesn’t belong there; it’s the wrong signal.”
	

	“And yet,” he adds, “because of the sisterhood and magic, I feel this is still classically Disney. If you’ve watched ‘Zombies’ and ‘Descendants’ and ‘Vampirina,’ and maybe you’re also dipping a toe into older genre shows, I think this is a bridge.”

	“Coven Academy” stars Malina Weissman as Briar, whose grief and anger about the unsolved murder of her mother, Mary, end up revealing a part of her identity she’d never known: She’s a witch. After reluctantly starting school in New Orleans, she befriends two fellow witches, Sasha (Jordan Leftwich) and Tegan (Ora Duplass), who teach her the ways of the magical world and help her search for answers about Mary (Cecilia Grace Deacon).
	

	That process requires the young witches to break some rules, attracting the watchful eye of the school’s headmaster, Miss Graves (Tiffani Thiessen), who they realize was close friends with Briar’s mother. Miss Graves’ secrecy, and some information shared by one of their teachers, Mr. Cole (Devon Sawa), lead them to believe that she’s the murderer. But it’s later revealed that the real Mr. Cole is locked in a basement. A shapeshifting Warlock named William — who turns out to be the father of the girls’ friend Jake (Malachi Barton) — has taken Mr. Cole’s place as part of a decades-long evil scheme. He had been friends with Mary back in school until she, Graves and their coven sister Tamora (Keegan Connor Tracy) thwarted his plan to pollute the ley lines, the mystical source of all witches’ and warlocks’ powers. The coven interrupted a spell he was casting that would have made it so that they could all use only dark magic, which would lead to the eradication of monsters like the werewolves that killed his family. Decades later, he had come out of hiding to try again, and didn’t hesitate to kill anyone in his way — including Mary.

	Briar, Sasha, Tegan and Graves — with an assist from Jake — manage to stop William and save the magical world. But as everyone processes their whirlwind semester at school, Briar can’t stop thinking about the connection she felt when Graves grabbed her hand to cast the spell on William. At the same time, Graves is shown speaking to Mary’s ghost in the woods. “I wanna tell her, Mary. She needs to know why I gave her up,” Graves says. “She needs to know what happened. No more secrets.” Mary replies, “No one can ever know you’re Briar’s birth mother. If the truth ever got out, you wouldn’t be able to protect her.” As a storm rolls in and Season 1 ends, Graves says, “She deserves to know.”

	Federle spoke to Variety about family secrets, the meaning behind dark magic and what’s to come for “Coven Academy.”

	
		“Coven Academy” isn’t based on IP, but you’re pulling from preexisting lore about witches, vampires and other mystical beings. What was your research process like? Did you create a rulebook about how magic operates in the world of the show?	

	Todd Slavkin and Darren Swimmer, my co-showrunners, ran “Shadowhunters” and “Smallville.” They really understand genre. And we staffed up the writers’ room primarily with women, and some of the younger women were on, like, their second viewing of “Vampire Diaries.” 

	In the room, we got pretty granular about the rules, like with warlocks and teleporting. I really wanted everything to be governed by character and emotion and what their perceived faults might be. For me, everything that got me picked on in middle school gets me paid now. I just needed to get with the right group, and then they would accept it. And for Briar, she gets labeled as angry or hot-headed, but it’s actually her source of power if she can channel it. For Tegan, it’s about having ADHD. It’s her ability to morph time, though other people might call her hyperactive. For Sasha, she is so empathic and has the ability to read other people, but she is not totally in touch with her own feelings. 

	All of those felt like metaphors for the teenage experience that could somehow be explored in magic. I wanted the magic to be driven by character.


	
		This show was originally intended to be Disney Channel’s first YA drama. It ended up moving to Freeform, but since you were writing with a Disney Channel audience in mind, how did you approach the level of violence, romance and darkness in the show?	

	So many young people, for better or for worse, are exposed to [mature themes]. When I was in high school myself, I was not reading the assigned reading; I was reading “The Shining.” There’s a curiosity about the darker, deeper experience of growing up. I think I have a pretty good internal barometer of what makes something Disney and appropriate for a younger audience, even if it toes the line. And when you look back, you’re like, “OK, Simba’s dad dying is traumatic.” The best Disney stories go to really genuine places, even if you’re not always seeing all the blood.

	But there is some blood and some making out in “Coven Academy.” I am very excited about a white space that I think exists at Disney. Disney has done the most incredible job of keeping an audience engaged through the [tween] era, but there’s this white space where I want to capture the audience — I don’t want them to go away. I’d like to see Disney really have a piece of that pie.




	

					Devon Sawa as Mr. Cole
	



	
		Let’s get into the plot now. Did you always know that the villain would be Jake’s dad, who Briar’s mom had a history with? Or were Graves or Cole ever real candidates?	

	Cole was never going to be the murderer. Devon Sawa is such a chameleon, so it was a joy to see him play multiple roles in one season. There was some discussion about Graves, but I liked the commonality and parallelism between Jake and Briar both having this giant parental question mark around them. And I kept bringing up, “What if Ms. Graves is actually her mom?” And the more I was watching Tiffani and Malina — their physical resemblance, and how maternal Tiffani is, as someone who grew up a teen icon — the more I felt like there was a really powerful story there. The idea that if a witch is related to another witch and they are in close proximity, there’s something very dangerous and powerful about that. That became the secret of the season, which I really hope we’re able to explore.


	
		Tell me more about William, the actual villain, and what his character represents.	

	The best villains think they’re heroes and that the thing they want is noble. He feels this very anti-monster stance. And in Jake’s awakening as a young warlock, he’s able to ultimately summon his father. “Coven Academy” is so much about: “Who are you if your family expects something? Who are you if you’re in the shadow of a sibling? Or if your family experiences trauma or loss? How do you make something out of that?” William is what happens if you go to the dark place. Genre is a blast, because you get to experiment with so much metaphor, whether it’s substance abuse or family shame. 


	
		The characters discuss the addictive nature of dark magic multiple times. Was it meant to stand in for substance abuse?	

	I hope the audience recognizes the idea that almost anything in moderation is OK, but be careful how deep you go. In my extended family, there’s some deep substance abuse, and I saw how it tore people apart and became a real emotional lightning rod. Dark magic is about that thing that you may be drawn to, whether it’s drinking or internet doomscrolling, that can be a perfectly benign habit, but if you go deep, it can take over.


	
		The tension between humans and “monsters” also seems to represent something bigger. It feels wrong when the witches and warlocks talk about vampires and werewolves like they aren’t equals, but it’s based on real fears about their safety. What were you trying to say with that conflict?	

	It’s definitely a commentary on othering. With McKenna [Sway Bhatia] getting bitten, we’re trying to figure out what that means for her story with Tegan. It’s a classic “Romeo and Juliet,” or any story about a group that feels different from you. Now more than ever, we’re so divided in so many ways, and it’s easy to write off a group of people. One of the reasons I wanted Ollie [Louis Thresher] to be a newly turned vampire was because it was truly thrust upon him. He did not walk out the door that morning and say, “I want to be a vampire.” Whereas Jake, the powerful warlock who’s got so much going for him, has darker qualities, in some ways, than Ollie, who is a genuinely great guy and is now trying to make the best of [his circumstances]. That’s the story of anybody growing up and deciding what kind of person they want to be. I don’t even think of the vampires as monsters. I keep using that word, but I think of them as just different — and aren’t we all different? I don’t like black-and-white stories. I like the gray.

	By the way, when Jake and Briar almost kiss in the final chapter, we also shot a version where they did kiss, and we were like, “We have to save this. This is a slow burn. We’re yearning. Don’t rush everything.” The gray is how you get 100 stories and not just 10.




	

					Malachi Barton as Jake, Malina Weissman as Briar
	



	
		There are also interesting gender politics going on. William warns Jake about witches getting together and being judgmental, and Jake has a line about how witches work together with their coven sisters, but warlocks deal with their problems on their own. 	

	I made a decision really early on to separate the witches and the warlocks. With the women, it’s about girlhood and sisterhood. They lean on each other and gossip and come back together. The guys are on this very solitary journey. In my mind — not addressed yet in the series — they all used to learn together. And then around ’98, when William made this decision that fractured the community forever, the well-meaning adults separated the genders. We are fully owning this idea that boys and men are just not as comfortable expressing themselves, and when they do, these days in particular, they’re listening to some potentially questionable sources. The young ladies in the show are calling each other out and keeping each other accountable. 

	At the beginning of the season, Briar doesn’t think of herself as a girl’s girl, and by the end, these are her sisters. Jake was being, if not brainwashed, certainly influenced by a male figure with some misogyny here. But Jake made a better decision than I think a lot of people do in real life.


	
		Thinking about a potential second season, how do you see Jake dealing the fact that he finally gained the father he’d been missing his whole life just to lose him again?	

	He has some major things to face when it comes to nature vs. nurture. “Am I always going to be drawn to dark magic? Is that my genetics?” It’s the addiction metaphor. But I would like to explore Mr. Cole being a genuine mentor to Jake moving forward. Jake is somebody who has to throw himself into something, because with idle time, he gets into trouble.


	
		What about Briar and Miss Graves? Thematically, what are you exploring by revealing they’re mother and daughter?	

	I’m childless, and I never wanted kids, but [in my work] I can’t graduate from high school, it seems. So I was interested in telling the story of a woman who absolutely knew her life would be complete without the experience of being a capital-M “Mother.” 

	Maybe it’s because I grew up a black sheep that I’m always drawn to stories of making your parents proud vs. following your own destiny. I liked the idea of suddenly looking at somebody anew and going, “Hold on a second. Like, if I’ve inherited X, Y and Z from you, what does that mean? Did you have anger issues too?” Secrets are a big thing in families. What you keep from your family to protect them ultimately creates bigger issues later. I don’t want to tell another straight-up mom mystery again, but I think there is something fun to explore in what makes a mother and daughter so dangerous when they’re together. And who would be most threatened by that?




	

					Tiffani Thiessen as Miss Graves
	




	
		What’s on your mind with the other characters as you contemplate a second season?	

	Ollie goes away because he doesn’t want to hurt Briar, yet he’s so drawn to her, and he recognizes the inherent unfairness of that. I think he’s going to work on if there’s a way back. Sasha’s desperately sad about her brother [Nathaniel Logan McIntyre] being a vampire and diving into this idea of, “Is there something I could do to turn him back? And if I could, would he even want that?” And Tegan’s got feelings developing for McKenna, who could very much be under threat. 

	I’m a selfish, greedy, ambitious showrunner. I don’t want to say seven seasons — I said that in every interview for “High School Musical: The Musical: The Series” and we got four, the longest running show on Disney+, I’ll humbly point out — but I’ve got similar ambitions for this. I’d love to create a world, and I hope the audience shows up.


	This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: Asghar Farhadi Says Films Like ‘Argo’ Perpetuate American White Savior Myth: ‘Who Asked You To Come and Save Us?’
description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Twice Oscar-winning filmmaker Asghar Farhadi, who is at the Rio Film Festival to present “Parallel Tales,” spoke about the
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Twice Oscar-winning filmmaker Asghar Farhadi, who is at the Rio Film Festival to present “Parallel Tales,” spoke about the perceived hegemony of American cinema and how Hollywood shouldn’t be seen as a source for faithful portrayals of foreign cultures.

	Asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A Separation” won Best International Film at the Oscars, Farhadi said he watched the film at the time it came out and felt it was a “Hollywood thing.” In the film, loosely based on a true story, director Ben Affleck plays a Latino exfiltration specialist who masquerades as a Hollywood producer to rescue six Americans held captive in Tehran during the U.S. hostage crisis in Iran. The moderator mentioned how Affleck’s film portrays Iran “like you’re in hell.”
	

	“The problem with these kinds of films in Hollywood [and] some people in the United States [is that] they look at the world from up to down,” he added. “Someday you should ask them: Why do you feel you’re up and we’re down? I don’t understand why they have this ego that they’re up.” The Iranian director then said Americans often claim to “have democracy,” but they don’t. “You don’t have democracy. It’s a lie.”


	Farhadi then recalled spending time in the U.S. a few years ago when working on a project and, during research, travelling to San Francisco to speak with incarcerated men. “I met some people in prison who are Black, [some who come] from other countries, and the real America was there. But people in the world don’t see that part of the United States.”
	

	“I have this problem when they feel they are up and they think, ‘[others] should be like us,’” he continued. “Even if it’s in a good way and they want to be kind to you, they wish ‘one day you’ll become like us,’ and no, I don’t want to.”

	Still on “Argo,” the director said movies like it “are not deep.” “They make these movies for money; it’s a business. And in these films it’s always a white guy from the United States saving others. My question is: Why? Why does an American go to Cuba or Iran to save people? People understand they can save themselves. Who asked you to come and save us?”

	Asked about how he broaches politics in his films, the renowned filmmaker said that, whenever “you talk about society, you are talking about politics.” “Even when you talk about family life, their relationships, their difficulties and problems, indirectly you are talking about politics. In my films, I always try not to talk about politics directly because, to me, that is a bit far from cinema. The cinema that I believe is the kind of cinema that gives space to audiences to discover things about themselves.”

	The director then brought up Abbas Kiarostami’s “Fellow Citizen” (“Hamshahri”) as Iran’s “most political film.” The 1983 documentary heavily trails drivers across the streets of the Iranian capital. “He made a documentary about car drivers in Tehran, but when you see people, the way they talk to the police, the layers are very political.”

	“Media and cinema don’t give you a complete image of people’s ordinary life,” he added. “But the thing about empathy is that, all around the world, people are similar to each other. Cinema is based on hate and love. And [when it comes to] hate and love, everywhere is the same. A love between a mother and child in Brazil, in Tehran, is the same. The way they express it is different, but the core is the same.”



	

					Parallel Tales
									Sydney Film Festival
	



	Farhadi said that when he watches a Brazilian film, he soon forgets he is watching a story from another place in the world, and feels it is a “film about us” as people. “If one day people can travel to other countries, and if they shake hands, that’s the best way to know people, not through media. I don’t believe media can give us the whole image.”
	

	On this, the filmmaker emphasized how his last two films, “A Hero” and “Parallel Tales,” are about how we see others and how we are seen in return. They are also heavily influenced by “how social media has shaped our lives.”

	“When we see something in the media, we should be careful,” he continued, adding that most information replicated by mainstream media about Iran, for example, comes from “very simple knowledge” of real life in the country. When a singular discourse is perpetuated, the director implied, it means people are “ready to accept” when someone says “they are the enemy.” “This is something the media is doing, because the most powerful media belongs to powerful people. This is the problem.”

	Farhadi spoke very briefly about his next film, reiterating it will be shot in his native language of Farsi. Enquired as to whether the film might deal with the current war in Iran and the conflict in Palestine, the director said: “Not directly,” suggesting the current political climate might have an underlying effect on the story despite not being the subject of his project.

	“The Salesman” helmer also recalled how “Parallel Tales” was supposed to be shot in the U.S. “I stayed there for three years, writing, searching, casting. I did casting in the U.S. with American actors, very big names. But every day that I came back to my home, I told myself: I cannot connect with this. Something is wrong. It was a big problem. One night I decided to change.”

	He said changing the film’s settings to France and moving production overseas was “not an easy decision,” but that “the DNA of this film is more European than American.”

	As for the starry cast that includes Isabelle Huppert, Virginie Efira and Vincent Cassel, the director said he sent the script to “select names” upon arriving in France, and he was “so lucky” because all of them immediately said yes. Still, when he goes to set, he doesn’t “think about names.” “All of them are my team, my family, my actors. It doesn’t matter if it’s a big name or not. The way I work is the same, and they like it.”

	The Rio Film Festival runs October 1-11.

title: 'Verity' Cast Reveals Their Book Recommendations on Heels of Novel's Big-Screen Adaptation (Exclusive)

	“Verity”
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	“Verity” is in theaters now, and based on projections, it could be the latest book-to-screen adaptation from author Colleen Hoover to top the box office charts. Now, the real-life cast of the romantic thriller are revealing what other books they enjoy, in an exclusive clip shared with Variety from Amazon News.

	Josh Hartnett, Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson sat down with Amazon for a rapid-fire Q&A game, where they shared thoughts on what makes a good book. As Hathaway explains, “Since ‘Verity’ is all about finishing a story, today we’re finishing a few sentences about the kinds of books we can’t put down.”


	Among their answers: Hathaway thinks a great book villain requires “a great inner monologue,” with the actress adding that, “it has to be somebody even if you’re not agreeing with what they’re saying, you want to listen to them.”

	Johnson, meantime, is asked what “‘Verity’ will have you questioning?” Her reply: “Your sexuality.”

	“Verity” features a twisted love triangle that begins after struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Johnson) is asked by Jeremy Crawford (Hartnett) to help finish a manuscript started by his now-comatose wife, the bestselling author Verity Crawford (Hathaway).

	Understandably, Hartnett says “Verity” could have you questioning “your partner” or at least lead to “some debate… by the end of [the book].” 

		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										READ THE BOOK						

					Verity		

	
		Collector’s Edition	
	
		First released in 2018, Hoover’s novel has returned to the top of the charts following the movie picture adaptation release. Amazon currently has the hardcover version of the book on sale. Readers can also find the book in Kindle Unlimited, with Amazon Prime members able to get three months of access for free (not a Prime member? Get a 30-day free trial here to access all the discounts and benefits).	
		
	

	The cast of “Verity,” meanwhile are also asked about what book recommendations they always trust, with Hathaway mentioning anything on the Man Booker Prize shortlist. Hartnett, meantime, shouts out a good friend who always “knows me” and “knows things.”




	Watch the full Q&A with the “Verity” cast above, and scroll for some book recommendations based on the actors’ answers from Amazon Books.

		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										GREAT VILLAINS						

					First Lie Wins: A Novel		

	
		Reese’s Book Club pick	
	
		One of Reese Witherspoon’s Book Club picks and a New York Times #1 Bestseller, “First Lie Wins” follows Evie Porter as she builds a life with her boyfriend, Ryan Sumner. The only problem: Porter isn’t who she says she is, and flashbacks reveal her murky history, including a shadowy boss she reports to known only as Mr. Smith.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										QUESTION YOUR PARTNER						

					The Housemaid		

	
		Adapted into feature film	
	
		Freida McFadden’s “The Housemaid” was adapted into a feature film in 2025 starring Amanda Seyfried and Sydney Sweeney. The psychological thriller (and BookTok fave) follows the housekeeper Millie Calloway (Sweeney) who begins working for the affluent Winchester family, only to uncover a history of lies and secrets.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										QUESTION YOUR SEXUALITY						

					Atmosphere: A Love Story		

	
		GMA Book Club pick	
	
		From Taylor Jenkins Reid, “Atmosphere” follows Joan Goodwin, one of the first female scientists to join NASA’s academy and part of a group of engineers preparing to go to space. Told through a present-day mission and past flashbacks, the novel explores everything from forbidden romances to female identify, as Joan fights to save her crew while navigating a (literal) whole new world.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										BOOKER PRIZE SHORTLIST						

					Flashlight: A Novel		

	
		National Book Award-winning author	
	
		Susan Choi’s “Flashlight” was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 2025 and was named one of the Best Books of the Year by more than a dozen publications. The novel begins with 10-year-old Louisa who is found alone and shivering after taking an evening walk along the water with her father, who only had a flashlight on him. Now, the family must piece together what happened that night, while navigating complicated feelings related to cultural identity and generational trauma.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

					Amazon
	
					
		

										BOOKER PRIZE SHORTLIST						

					The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny: A Novel		

	
		NYT 10 Best Books of 2025	
	
		Sonia and Sunny randomly encounter each other on an overnight train in India during a hiatus from their new lives in the U.S. But it turns out they have been introduced previously before, and their chance meeting resparks buried feelings and admissions. As a book description teases, the novel touches on “country, class, race, history and the complicated bonds that link one generation to the next.”Hartnett says he picks up books based on a trusted recommendation: this book was listed as a favorite by none other than Barack Obama.	
		
	

	“Verity” is in theaters now and you can buy the book online on Amazon. You can browse more bestsellers and also find thousands of titles discounted for Prime Big Deal Days on the Amazon book hub here.

title: Jerry Golod, Producer of ‘Tales From the Darkside’ and Former CBS And NBC Executive, Dies at 87
description: Jerry Golod, the producer of “Tales From the Darkside,” died following a brief battle with cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif., on Wednesday
body:
Jerry Golod, the producer of “Tales From the Darkside,” died following a brief battle with cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif., on Wednesday. He was 87.

	Throughout his career, Golod served as an executive at CBS and NBC, later launching JayGee Productions in the early 1980s. After seeing the success of Stephen King’s 1982 film “Creepshow,” Golod collaborated with director Romero and producer Richard P. Rubinstein to bring the narrative to television. The three of them went on to launch “Tales From the Darkside,” which ran for four seasons and garnered a high cult following.
	

	He also helped launch “Adderly” after reading Elliott Baker’s 1971 book, “Pocock and Pitt,” and becoming intrigued by the secondary character of the same name. The adventure series starred Winston Rekert and ran for two seasons on CBS.


	In 1975, Golod became vice president of children’s programs at CBS before moving to NBC Entertainment in 1979 as vice president and national program director. While there, he oversaw daytime and children’s programming, specials, variety and West Coast late-night programming. He later joined CBS Television Studios and The CW in developing a new revival of “Tales From the Darkside,” though the series never moved past a 2015 pilot.

	Golod executive produced CBS’s “Brass” in 1985 and “Return to Green Acres,” which reunited cast members of the 1960s sitcom. He also executive produced the 1991 revival of “Land of the Lost,” which ran for two seasons.

	Golod was born in the Bronx on Dec. 26, 1938, and graduated from City College of New York. He began his career at advertising agency Dancer Fitzgerald Sample and went on to become vice president and associate director of programming. He also spent three years overseeing a television production company affiliated with the agency.
	

	In the ‘90s, Golod worked with Pet Television Network as co-chairman and co-owner of a cable and satellite service aimed toward animal enthusiasts.

	Golod is survived by his wife of 59 years, Ruth; their children, Dori and Jason; son-in-law Doug; daughter-in-law Danielle; grandchildren Gavin, Ramey, Morgan and Madison; great-grandsons Everett and Winslow; and nieces and nephews Jill, David, Elise, Renee, Celia, Ari and Ava.

title: Aaron Sorkin Says It ‘Never Occurred’ to Him That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Play Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Claims the Paycheck Was a ‘Disincentive’
description: Before Jesse Eisenberg declined to step back into the world of Facebook as Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” the director a
body:
Before Jesse Eisenberg declined to step back into the world of Facebook as Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” the director admitted “it never occurred” to him that the actor wouldn’t be on board with his 2026 follow-up to 2010’s “The Social Network,” in which Eisenberg portrayed the young tech billionaire.

	Speaking with Entertainment Weekly, Sorkin recounted that he was “just a couple of pages from being done” with the script for the new film when he ran into Eisenberg at a party, “and said, ‘I’m gonna be sending you something in a couple of weeks.’” The actor “smiled and nodded, and I sent it to him,” said Sorkin. “It never occurred to me that he wouldn’t wanna do it.”
	

	Sorkin continued, explaining he tried to convince the “A Real Pain” actor, but he didn’t budge.


	“This is the only time I’ve written myself an outline. I don’t do it for the movies, but I did it for my conversations with Jesse,” he said. “It was arguments for why he should do it. They included, ‘We already know you’re gonna be great because you were already once.’ You know, ‘Here are the great moments that you’re gonna get to play in the movie.’ And I laid it out for him.” And while Eisenberg didn’t sign on, he did tell Sorkin that their conversations made him “come closer to changing my mind than I thought you were going to,” which the director said “pleased” him.

	Not even a sizeable paycheck could sway Eisenberg, admitted Sorkin. “I knew what the studio was offering him to do it, but money does not motivate Jesse. It’s infuriating,” said Sorkin. “If anything, money is a disincentive for him. It’s admirable. He’s very concerned about raising his kids with too much money.”
	

	In the lead-up to the release of “The Social Reckoning,” which hits theaters on Oct. 9, Eisenberg’s refusal to return as Zuckerberg has been a hot topic. (“Succession” actor Jeremy Strong stars as the Facebook founder instead.) Speaking with Variety, the actor said: “I just told [Sorkin] I’m moving in different directions in my life, and you know, what he said sums it up nicely. I don’t want to be associated with that character, but all of my reasons for not wanting to do the movie have nothing to do with how wonderful the movie is, and will be, and I’m sure is already.”

	“The Social Network,” which also starred Andrew Garfield and Justin Timberlake, was nominated for eight Oscars and won three, including best adapted screenplay for Sorkin, best film editing and best original score. Eisenberg earned an Oscar nomination for his portrayal of Zuckerberg. “The Social Reckoning” stars Strong, Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Billy Magnussen, Bill Burr and more.

schema.headline: Aaron Sorkin Says It ‘Never Occurred’ to Him That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Play Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Claims the Paycheck Was a ‘Disincentive’

title: Box Office: ‘Digger’ Nosediving With $3.4 Million on Opening Day, ‘Verity’ Lands at No. 1 With $15.1 Million on Friday
description: Not even a Tom Cruise-filled, all-stops-pulled press tour — including a GQ cover, a “New Heights” podcast appearance and a “Risky Business”-inspired
body:
Not even a Tom Cruise-filled, all-stops-pulled press tour — including a GQ cover, a “New Heights” podcast appearance and a “Risky Business”-inspired jaunt down the “Jennifer Hudson Show” spirit tunnel — could keep “Digger” from flatlining at the box office.

	Warner Bros.’ R-rated black comedy generated $3.4 million from 3,321 North American theaters on Friday following a slew of negative reviews and divided word of mouth. The film is shaping up to be one of the year’s biggest flops, with estimates of just $7.5 million domestically in its opening weekend. The film was greenlit at $125 million but ended up ballooning to $160 and $180 million after production ran long, according to knowledgeable sources. That’s a problem because the studio splits ticket sales with theater owners, meaning “Digger” is primed to lose many millions in its theatrical run.
	

	Directed by Academy Award winner Alejandro González Iñárritu, “Digger” stars Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon whose company sparks an ecological calamity. Despite Cruise’s enduring star power, having anchored recent blockbusters like the “Mission: Impossible” franchise and 2022’s sensation “Top Gun: Maverick,” “Digger” will wind up as the latest misfire for Warner Bros. This year, the studio has siphoned off a string of duds including Maggie Gyllenhaal’s punk rock “The Bride!” and DC’s comic book adaptation “Supergirl.”

	With general audiences rejecting “Digger,” Amazon MGM’s psycho-thriller “Verity” took the top spot on Friday with $15.1 million from 3,510 North American theaters. The movie is expected to make $33.6 million domestically through the weekend.
	

	Adapted from Colleen Hoover’s bestselling book of the same name, “Verity” centers around famed author Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), who gets badly injured in a car accident, leaving her husband (Josh Hartnett) to hire a struggling writer (Dakota Johnson) to finish the remaining books. Michael Showalter directed. It’s Hoover’s fourth novel to hit the big screen, following 2024’s “It Ends With Us” (Sony), 2025’s “Regretting You” (Paramount), and 2026’s “Reminders of Him” (Universal).

	Zach Cregger’s zombie horror “Resident Evil” landed in second place on Friday, grossing $3.62 million. Starring Austin Abrams as a medical courier who must contend with a zombie outbreak while making a delivery to Raccoon City General Hospital, the Sony film looks to add $12 million by Sunday, bringing its domestic total to $124.395 million. 

	After “Digger’s” third-place finish, Paramount Pictures’ “The Heart of the Beast” followed with $3.15 million, bringing its cumulative gross to $38.39 million. The Brad Pitt-led adventure film was directed by David Ayer and stars the actor as a retired veteran who navigates a 58-mile trek to safety after he and his combat dog survive a plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness.

	Finally, in fifth, was A24’s “Primetime.” The film grossed $2.49 million on Friday and should pull in another $7.5 million by Sunday. The film’s opening weekend registered as the third-best for A24 behind “Backrooms” ($81.4 million) and “Civil War” ($25.5 million), and the Robert Pattinson-led drama has pulled in $28.58 million domestically thus far. 

	“Primetime” chronicles Chris Hansen’s time as the host of Dateline NBC’s “To Catch a Predator.” While the film has received positive reviews and word of mouth since its debut at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, the real-life Hansen has been less than complimentary ahead of the film’s release; after seeing the film, Hansen called it “so bizarre and so in-and-out of reality,” as well as “detached from reality.”

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Digger’ Nosediving With $3.4 Million on Opening Day, ‘Verity’ Lands at No. 1 With $15.1 Million on Friday

title: ‘Behemoth!’: Why Tony Gilroy Needed Nine Composers to Score His Latest Film, and a Guide to Who Did What in the Film (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Behemoth!” in theaters Dec. 4

	Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” bowed at the New York Film Festival
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Behemoth!” in theaters Dec. 4

	Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” bowed at the New York Film Festival Friday, and Lincoln Center’s Tully Hall seemed a fitting place to showcase a film about a musician.

	Written and directed by Gilroy, the film stars Pedro Pascal as a cellist who returns to Los Angeles after a life on the road. Music is in his DNA — his parents were musicians, as were his grandparents. Music serves as a storytelling device, with Alex’s performances, whether on stage or in films he worked on, triggering flashbacks that reveal why he left Hollywood and what brought him back.
	

	Gilroy wanted distinct scores for each film Alex works on. Rather than rely on a single composer, Gilroy turned to nine composers: Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandon Roberts and Alan Silvestri, known as the Behemoth Collective, to deliver distinct cues for the fictional movies Alex works on. In doing so, each composer brought their unique voices to the film.

	Speaking with Variety, Gilroy explains that he had been sitting with the idea for years. He recalled the first time he walked into the John Williams Scoring Stage, steeped in Hollywood history. “You get in there, and there’s the emotional power and the smell of that room. It’s such a place of work, and then this incredible magic thing happens and there’s no place for the music to go except into the microphones and into your ears. It can’t escape that room.”
	

	He went on to say, “It’s a vivid emotional trigger and I just kept wondering every time I went there — why didn’t anybody make a movie about this? Every time I went, I was like, ‘God, there’s got to be a movie here somewhere.’ I couldn’t figure it out.”

	Eventually, he did. 

	He wrote a script that is a love letter to movie music and the art of scoring, carefully curating a story that allowed him to seamlessly integrate the work of the Behemoth Collective into the film.

	Gilroy didn’t want one composer. “I knew I had to have different voices, and once you’re going to open it up, you want to cast it like actors,” he explains. “I made backstories for all the shows, so all the shows have a story to them and I could tell all the composers what the plots of their show were.” With that he started going out to composers. “Henry Jackman was the first one who came on, and he was so enthusiastic from the beginning. He gave me the enthusiasm to keep going forward with it. I talked to some people that I knew. I knew I wanted Michael Giacchino for the cartoon cue. I knew that I’d bring Brandon back,” and so the collective eventually came together.

	Variety spoke with all nine composers to break down their cues and the key instruments they used to bring the “Behemoth!” score together.

	Michael Abels

	Abels was tasked with composing the music for Alex’s solo cello practice sessions. In one scene, Alex practices in a room and the music transitions into a flashback of Alex as a six-year-old prodigy performing Bach’s Cello Prelude No. 1 on “The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson.” Abels explains, “The music morphs from a warm-up exercise into the actual Bach piece.”

	Emily Bear

	Bear wrote the love theme for “Season of Glass.” She says, “It’s inspired by the French and Italian film scores of the ’60s: a lot of lush strings, beautiful harmonics, a lot of jazz-inspired progressions, but in an orchestral setting.”

	Gilroy provided a detailed backstory for the fictional film, describing a young widow, a wealthy East Coast summer setting and a boy preparing to go to war. Bear also wrote a waltz for a scene where the young widow teaches the boy to dance. Bear notes, “It’s this very intimate, slow, tentative waltz that has some contention building underneath, so we added a lot of counterpoint and weird chromatic stuff underneath.”
	

	Lukas Frank

	Frank composed the film’s original song, “Your God Is Sleeping,” as well as the “Serian Suite,” which is tied to Alex’s character. “The suite is the underscore that opens throughout. It comes in throughout,” Frank explains.

	The prepared piano was a key element of the “Serian Suite.” “There’s someone drilling on a string to make this low droning sound,” Frank notes. “The whole movie opens with the sound of the pedal coming down off the piano, and then some simple strings come in.”

	Michael Giacchino

	Giacchino wrote music using a standard orchestra for the cartoon “Happy & Slappy,” which Alex’s father composed during his career.

	“I had to write a cue that his father wrote for these cartoons back in the ’60s cartoon, similar to ’Tom and Jerry,’” Giacchino explains. The music is used in a scene where Alex watches his brother fight while the cartoon score plays, syncing humorously with the action.

	Henry Jackman

	Jackman created the music for “Spies Don’t Run,” another fictional film within the story. Jackman describes it as “slightly ‘Jason Bourne-ish’, with a Middle Eastern flavor.”

	Jackman’s work involved multiple scoring sessions. But for “Spies Don’t Run,” he took to it seriously and ended up scoring a six-minute suite using “a combination of orchestra, a little bit of slightly abstracted vocals, with quite a lot of heavy percussion.”

	Nami Melumad

	Melumad contributed the cue for one of the films within the film, “Tolerance Hill.” She explains that Gilroy’s guidance helped shape her approach. “Tony described it as a period film within the story, but it also had to emotionally lead us through Alex, the main character, as he revisits his childhood home.”

	Melumad turned to the harp, an instrument Alex’s mother played, to evoke warmth, nostalgia and sadness. “It’s very delicate,” she says.

	James Newton Howard

	Howard composed the emotional finale of the film. “It’s pure underscore — a solo piano expressing the sadness of what’s happening in the story,” he says. Howard created multiple variations, including a piano-and-cello duet and orchestral arrangements. “It’s where everything comes together,” he notes.
	

	Brandon Roberts

	Roberts was tasked with writing “Look Away Jones,” a piece intended to sound like music Alex’s father had written for a TV show. Roberts says Gilroy described it as a “full-on smoking jazz band theme song for this make-believe show about an ex-football star turned detective.” 

	To prepare, Roberts listened to a lot of Quincy Jones and other theme music from that era. “It was an issue of coming up with a theme that felt like it actually existed and could have been on network television at the time,” he explains.

	Roberts collaborated with renowned flute player Katisse Buckingham, who played jazz flute and Tim Liu, who assembled a group of musicians. “They knocked it out of the park,” Roberts says.

	Alan Silvestri 

	Silvestri composed the cue that plays during the scoring session for “Open World,” a big Hollywood blockbuster and is a decoy title for a fictional production called “Behemoth.” It then bleeds from the scoring session into a sequence in the film. Silvestri describes it as a “big caper moment.” He adds, “I approached it as if it were a high-stakes adventure.”

	Silvestri used a large orchestra to create a score that played the heist completely straight, despite its humorous premise.

	Watch the trailer below.

schema.headline: ‘Behemoth!’: Why Tony Gilroy Needed Nine Composers to Score His Latest Film, and a Guide to Who Did What in the Film (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Zach Bryan Wears ‘Free Palestine’ Shirt While Headlining Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium; Drummer Honors Slain Palestinian Girl
description: Macklemore may have been barred from saying “Free Palestine!” at Robert Kraft‘s Gillette Stadium — and indeed, from anywhere else on Ed Sheeran‘s t
body:
Macklemore may have been barred from saying “Free Palestine!” at Robert Kraft‘s Gillette Stadium — and indeed, from anywhere else on Ed Sheeran‘s tour, as that headliner agreed with Kraft that the controversial rapper should be removed from the opening slot on all the shows he was booked for. But it was probably inevitable that, at some point, some musician would make a statement by sneaking in the same message while playing Kraft’s venue in Foxborough, Mass.

	What was surprising, to just about everyone, was who actually pulled it off: Zach Bryan. The country-rock superstar wore a “Free Palestine” T-shirt Friday night in the first of his two headlining appearances at Gillette Stadium, and fan footage shared from the venue’s big screens shows that at least two of Bryan’s band members were wearing Palestine jerseys as well.

	Part of the surprise in Bryan being the one to make the bold statement in Kraft territory is that he is a proud Navy veteran working at least on the outskirts of a genre, country, that has a fan base that would not be universally welcoming to such a position. Indeed, the reaction among self-proclaimed Bryan fans on X and other social media platforms was deeply riven, as word of his wardrobe choice spread late Friday night and into Saturday morning.

	Bryan was seen wearing a T-shirt (with the sleeves cut off, as is his nightly custom) bearing the logo “Free Palestine.” Beneath that on the shirt were an emblem of a pine tree and another message that read “An Appeal to Heaven.” These are references to a flag commissioned by George Washington in 1775 for a fleet of schooners sent to intercept British ships; later, it became the flag for the Massachusetts Navy — giving it a distinct historical and local connection for the Boston-area show.

	Bryan’s drummer, Nate Head bore a jersey with Palestine on the front and, on the back, the numeral 5 and the name “Hind Rajab.” Rajab was a 5-year-old girl in Gaza reported to have been killed by the Israeli military’s tank fire on Jan. 24, 2024, after having been trapped with her cousin and pleading for help in a disabled car for hours. 



	

					Big-screen image of Zach Bryan’s drummer wearing pro-Palestine shirt
									X
	



	On his Instagram Stories, the drummer reposted a user sharing footage of him pounding the drums while wearing his Palestine/Hind Rajab jersey, with that user’s caption, “Who wants to listen to me talk for 2 hours straight about this cultural shift,” and the hashtags “RIP Hind Rajab” and “Free Palestine.”



	

	



	Bryan’s guitarist, Noah Le Gros, also wore a green Palestine soccer jersey. He was later seen posing, pointedly, in front of a Kraft Sports & Entertainment sign backstage.




	

	



	Some news outlets ran with a widely spread and apparently false statement attributed to Bryan on Saturday. The statement, in which Bryan supposedly spoke up defending his stance from the night before, came from an X account that purports to belong to the singer but does not. (Bryan’s real X account has been deactivated.)


	Bryan and band are set to perform at Gillette Stadium for a second consecutive night on Saturday evening. A Ticketmaster seating chart for the show indicates only a few hundred tickets still on sale for the show, in a venue with an estimated concert capacity of 70,000.
	

	Bryan’s on-stage statement immediately drew a lot of negative feedback from conservative fans, although there are pockets on the right that have come out against Israel’s actions in Gaza who applauded Bryan. Among them was Candace Owens, who posted on X, “This is amazing. Only made more amazing by the fact that Zach Bryan served our country. Genocide is always wrong.”


	Bryan’s politics have been somewhat elusive, with the singer-songwriter posting that he finds deep problems on both sides of America’s political divides. He previously raised the ire of some on the right with a song titled “Bad News,” which among its scattershot character-study lyrics, contained a seemingly negative reference to ICE (“ICE is gonna come, bust down your door / Try and build a house no one builds no more / But I got a telephone / Kids are all scared and all alone”). Following that, many on social media threatened to “Bud Light” him — that is, subject him to a boycott. But Bryan’s stadium shows have continued to be sellouts, and the artist has remained mostly apolitical as far as taking stands on any hot-button issues.

	It has been just under a month since Macklemore spoke out against Israel opening for Ed Sheeran’s “Loop” tour at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sept. 4. Although the tour promoter believed he had agreed to not repeat the statements the following night, he did, leading to his dismissal from the tour. Messina Touring Group, the promoter, said that Kraft — a friend of Sheeran — would not allow the tour to play his venues if Macklemore remained on the bill. (Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium ended up being canceled anyway, due to the east coast’s damaging nor’easter weather.)
	

	Attempts to reach Robert Kraft’s organization for comment Saturday were unsuccessful.

	A smattering of social media reactions to Bryan’s T-shirt statement:

	“Zach Bryan is a pussy and an embarrassment to our military and veterans. From the river to the sea, Palestine is debris.” (from noreallystfu)

	“Here is Oologah, Oklahoma’s favorite son playing ‘Oklahoma Smokeshow’ in a Free Palestine shirt at Gillette Stadium. He might not be playing that second Gillette show tonight and he definitely won’t be making any Sonic ads, but.. The balls on Zach Bryan… who knew?” (AshleyTXBurner)

	“Fucking amazing, Zach Bryan is on the right side of history. Everyone knows Israel has been committing genocide and ethnic cleansing, and the entire world and the American people will not stay silent. Free Palestine.” (RealDea87170572)

	“This will be career ending for him, he is just up his own that much that he doesn’t see it. Maren Morris found out the hard way. His actual fans are RIGHT WING, not leftwing. He’s now BFFs with that other closet case Jew hater, Bruce Springsteen. He’s anti-Trump, anti-Ice, anti-MAGA.” (Tradwife2222)

	“IT’S OFFICIAL: Country singer Zach Bryan just went full 3rd world Islamist sympathizer and is getting the JELLY ROLL treatment after exposing his true colors. ‘Free Palestine.’ Go live there, so stunning and brave! He’s just more Hollywood BS. Virtue signaling to leftists!” (EricLDaugh) 
	

	“Robert Kraft has now banned him from using razors.” (mchooyah)

	“Kraft can have all the tantrums he likes but I very much doubt he’ll be able to bully Zach Bryan into submission. This is a clear act of defiance and an F you to both Kraft and Sheeran.” (DisparatePanda)

	“Zach Bryan served 8 years active duty in the United States military and I’m reading tweets for him to be deported. If that doesn’t tell you everything you need to know I’m not sure what does.” (HamoodyJafar)

	“Another Cuck for Islam.” (tjtradez2080)

	“Dear Ed Sheeran, If you ever need to borrow some fucking balls for standing up for what’s right Zach Bryan has more than enough to go around!” (ItsThatGuy330)

	“Zach Bryan rolled into Gillette Stadium, looked at a sold-out country crowd that drove hours to hear songs about trucks and bad decisions, and decided what they really needed was a foreign-policy seminar. … Country radio didn’t get big because the parking lot was full of people looking for a lecture on Gaza. Most of that crowd doesn’t support Palestine, doesn’t want the shirt, and didn’t ask the guy with the guitar to settle the Middle East between encores. But the shirt went on anyway. That’s the modern move. You get famous off one audience, then you borrow somebody else’s politics and act surprised when half the room stops clapping.” (wickedsmaahht)

	“A real Spartacus moment in music. All true artists resist conformity and control. Trying to tell the most recalcitrant people what they can or can’t say was always going to backfire. This trend will only grew the more there is an attempt to censor. Bravo, Zach Bryan and crew!” (im_PULSE)

	“Siri, add Zach Bryan to my Spotify playlist.” (MrWobbleWubMstr)

title: Zach Bryan's Drummer Wears 'Palestine' Jersey With Special Meaning
description:
Zach Bryan's Drummer

body:
Zach Bryan's Drummer
                          I Support Zach ... Just Look at My Shirt!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 3, 2026
                            7:40 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Zach Bryan's drummer joined in on his pro-Palestinian outfit choice at Robert Kraft's Gillette Stadium ... by wearing a jersey with a special meaning.
      
    
      
      Zach Bryan and members of his band, including his drummer and guitarist, took a defiant stand on October 2, 2026, by wearing "Free Palestine" and "Hind Rajab" shirts during their concert at Robert Kraft's Gillette Stadium. The Palestine Jersey worn by the guitarist, and Hind… pic.twitter.com/5hVsIBYbwU
              @TheGroundIntel
          
  
    
            Musician Nate Head wore a white and tan striped "Palestine" jersey with the name Hind Rajab on the back and the number 5.
      
    
            Rajab was a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed in January 2024 after the Israeli military opened fire on the car she was in as her family tried to flee Israeli evacuation orders ... according to Al Jazeera.
      

      
      We are so honored to see musician Noah Le Gros rocking our Palestine Jersey on stage at the Gillette Stadium (owned by Robert Kraft, the same guy who called Ed Sheeran to kick Macklemore off the tour) Noah and Zach both stood for Palestine tonight on a stage that tried to ban… pic.twitter.com/tssgB43ZyQ
              @WearThePeaceCo
  
    
            Guitarist Noah Le Gros also joined in on the statement ... and wore a green jersey with "Palestine" written on it as well.
      
    
            The shirts and jersey are apparently from Wear the Peace -- an organization that donates to programs and humanitarian efforts in Gaza.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we reported, Bryan and his band donned the outfits during their first of 2 nights of performances at the stadium in Foxborough, MA.
      
    
            His next upcoming night show as part of his "With Heaven On" tour is set for 7 PM tonight ... we'll see what they wear this evening!
      
    
            As you know ... Kraft played a large part in having Macklemore kicked off of Ed Sheeran's tour after he made pro-Palestinian remarks during 2 shows in New Jersey.

body:
Alleged Cornell Gang Rape
                          D.A. Turned Down More Evidence From Cops
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 3, 2026
                            5:13 AM PDT
                                                                      |

                                  October 3, 2026
                                7:41 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The D.A. who oversaw the alleged Cornell gang rape case denied the chance to review additional evidence during the initial investigation ... according to a new report.
      
    
            Tompkins District Attorney Matt Van Houten has been adamant that campus police only gave him Jane Doe's sworn statement and a screen grab of the alleged Chi Phi Snapchat messages -- but now it turns out his office turned down the opportunity to review additional statements ... the New York Times reported.
      
    
            Cornell University Police Department investigator Jeffrey Northrop spoke to a member of the D.A.'s staff, Jeff Huddle, about additional interviews ... according to records obtained by the NYT.
      
    
            Prosecutors reportedly didn't have any interest, however -- the outlet says Northrop took notes of the meeting and claimed prosecutors told him that "criminal charges would not be pursued in this case" based on Jane Doe's statement.
      
    
            This is quite a departure from what Van Houten previously said about why he declined to pursue charges.
      
    
            We reported earlier ... Van Houten claimed that he never received the full transcript of Jane Doe's 2-day interview from campus police.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            While Van Houten had said that he'd present evidence in front of a grand jury ... New York Governor Kathy Hochul has since appointed Attorney General Letitia James to take over the case.
      
    
            We've reached out to Van Houten for comment ... so far, no word back.

            A child pop star who was a trainee of the Japanese girls’ idol group DIANNA Project has died. She was only 8 years old.
      
    
            Hirata Runa "passed away peacefully" on Sept. 25 ... according to her X account.
      
    
            The DIANNA Project shared in a statement that the up-and-comer died "due to myocarditis resulting from influenza."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The group -- which asked for privacy on behalf of the family -- added ... "We extend our heartfelt thanks to all the fans who supported Runa Hirata and to everyone involved who provided their support."
      

            Following her last performance -- which took place on Sept. 20, according to The Standard -- Runa wrote ... "Thank you for today too, I appreciate it. It was so much fun."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Just 8 days later, her team wrote on her X account ... "To all the fellow idols who were kind to Ruyu during her lifetime, to the fans who supported Ruyu, to everyone at the agency who made Ruyu an idol, and to all the people who were involved with Ruyu, thank you very much."
      
    
            Myocarditis is inflammation of the middle muscular layer of the heart wall, called the myocardium ... according to the American Heart Association.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She was only 8 years old.
